concepts.def: A fundamental particle (up, down, strange, charm, top, bottom) that makes up hadrons.
A fundamental particle not subject to the strong interaction; includes the electron, muon and neutrinos.
A composite particle made of quarks; subdivided into baryons (3 quarks) and mesons (quark-antiquark).

walkthroughs.body_html:
Foundations of Physics — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Foundations of Physics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Foundations of Physics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

options: udd
uud
uds
uuu

mcqs.q: In β⁻ decay, the exchange particle is:
options: Photon
W⁻ boson
Gluon
Z boson

mcqs.q: Does light always travel at the same speed?
options: DC cannot enter a transformer because the iron core blocks it.
Only in a vacuum; in any material medium (water, glass) light travels more slowly, which is what causes refraction.
No — light always slows with distance from its source.
Yes — c is a universal constant in every situation.

mcqs.q: Why do transformers only work with alternating current?
options: It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
Transformers work with DC too, just less efficiently.
A transformer needs a changing magnetic flux in the core; DC produces a steady flux and so no emf is induced in the secondary.
DC cannot enter a transformer because the iron core blocks it.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two masses doubles, what happens to the gravitational force between them?
options: It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
It quarters — gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
No — light always slows with distance from its source.
It halves — gravitational force is inversely proportional to distance.
